When you run a large language model on a single computer, the bottleneck is usually not how fast the processor can do math, but how fast it can move data. This is known as the memory bandwidth limit.

To understand why, consider what happens when the model generates a single new word. The model has billions of parameters (weights). To calculate the next word, the computer must load all those weights from the main memory (RAM or VRAM) into the processor’s fast, temporary cache. Once the weights are loaded, the processor performs a massive amount of multiplication and addition operations.

Here is the key issue: for a single user, the "batch size" is effectively one. This means the processor is doing a huge amount of work for every single piece of data it moves. In technical terms, this results in a low "arithmetic intensity." The processor spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory, rather than actually calculating. It is like a chef who has a super-fast knife (high FLOPs) but can only get one ingredient at a time from a slow pantry (low memory bandwidth). The chef spends 90% of the time walking to the pantry and only 10% of the time chopping.

If you were running the model for thousands of users at once (a large batch), the processor could reuse the same loaded weights for many different inputs. This would increase the amount of math done per byte of data moved, making the processor the bottleneck instead. But for a single user, that reuse doesn’t happen.

Therefore, even if you have a processor capable of trillions of calculations per second, if it can only pull data from memory at a certain speed, the total speed of the model is capped by that memory transfer rate. Upgrading to a faster processor won’t help much if the memory bus is too slow. This is why, for single-user inference, memory bandwidth is the critical factor determining how fast the model can respond.

from typing import Any, Dict


def p(d: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, str]:
    """
    Filter and normalize a dictionary.

    Removes entries whose values are None or empty strings,
    then converts the remaining values to lowercase, stripped strings.
    The resulting dictionary is sorted by key.

    Args:
        d: A dictionary with string keys and arbitrary values.

    Returns:
        A new dictionary with filtered, normalized, and sorted entries.
    """
    return {
        k: str(v).strip().lower()
        for k, v in d.items()
        if v is not None and v != ''
    }
